candidates.label: Syrtis Maior (Gulf of Sidra)
candidates.support: A gulf on the northern coast of Africa, off today's Libya, known in ancient geography as Syrtis Maior, whose sandbanks sailors long feared as a hazard; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Roman poet Virgil refers to the danger in the Aeneid. Acts 27:17 says the storm-driven ship's crew, fearing they would run aground there, lowered the sea anchor instead; the ship never reached it. OpenBible.info identifies the Syrtis of Acts 27:17 with the Gulf of Sidra, which Wikidata and Pleiades equate with ancient Syrtis Maior; their points lie about 17 km apart, close for a gulf this size.

summary.text: Syrtis, known in ancient geography as Syrtis Maior and today as the Gulf of Sidra, is a broad gulf on the North African coast. Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography describes its waters as dangerous to navigate because of shallows and submerged rocks, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that sailors long regarded it as a source of danger, as the Roman poet Virgil describes in the Aeneid. Acts records that when a violent storm drove Paul's ship off course near Crete, the crew, fearing they would run aground on the Syrtis sand bars, lowered the sea anchor and let the ship drive before the wind instead; the ship never actually reached the gulf.

history.text: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography describes Syrtis Maior as one of two gulfs on the North African coast, the smaller Syrtis Minor lying further west. It states that the coastal tract between the two, called Syrtica Regio, at first belonged to the Cyrenaeans but was later taken by Carthage, becoming part of the Roman province of Africa once Carthage fell to Rome. Its separate entry on Cyrenaica, the district around Cyrene that the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places within the Roman province of Crete and Cyrene, states that after long disputes Cyrenaica's own western boundary was fixed at the bottom of the Great Syrtis, whose waters washed its shore.

scripture.textWEB: After they had hoisted it up, they used cables to help reinforce the ship. Fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis sand bars, they lowered the sea anchor, and so were driven along.

politicalHistory.entity: A sailing hazard off the North African coast, at the boundary between the Roman province of Africa (to the west, not otherwise shown on this map) and Cyrenaica, within the Roman province of Crete and Cyrene; this feature has no single political area of its own on this map.
